levels.title: Hospitalised Patient Nursing: Reading Depth, Comfort and Continuity

units.title: Anaesthesia Depth, Pain and the Recovery Room

lessons.title: Anaesthetic depth is a pattern, not a single number
lessons.explanation: Depth of anaesthesia is a continuum of central nervous system depression, and reading it is a technician skill built from several channels of evidence rather than one measurement. The classic teaching, Guedel's signs and stages, was described in the 1930s for ether anaesthesia in cats: stage one excitement, stage two involuntary struggling, a third stage with light, medium and deep planes, and a fourth stage of respiratory arrest. Veterinary teaching material is explicit that with modern inhalation agents, concurrent injectable drugs and neuromuscular blockers these classic signs do not fit well, and that the modern concept is often reduced to two states, awake and unconscious. That is not a reason to abandon structure; it is a reason to read a pattern. The signs a technician combines are nerve reflexes, muscle tone and eye signs: the palpebral reflex, the corneal reflex, the pupillary light reflex, jaw tone, eyeball position, lacrimation and the swallowing reflex. Each behaves differently across species, and the Western University teaching notes say so directly. The palpebral reflex varies between species, and dogs may have no palpebral reflex at an adequate surgical depth, whereas complete loss in a horse indicates moderately deep anaesthesia. The corneal reflex does not disappear until deep anaesthesia and should always be present. Nystagmus usually indicates excitement and a light plane, but dissociative agents such as ketamine cause nystagmus at moderate depth, and in horses severe hypoxia or hypercapnia can cause it too, where the correct interpretation is not light anaesthesia but a patient in trouble. A medioventral eyeball position is the most desirable in most species but not in horses, where a central position is expected, and moderate to loose jaw tone is what a team wants to feel. The signs that matter most are responses to stimulation: gross purposeful movement, reflex movement to a stimulus, an immediate cardiovascular response such as a sudden marked rise in heart rate or blood pressure, an immediate respiratory response, and any response to handling before the incision, during clipping, surgical preparation, draping or clamp placement. The same notes classify heart rate alone as a less reliable sign, because it may rise or fall, and may rise to compensate for a falling stroke volume even in a deep plane. Practical monitoring guidance from a University of Edinburgh teaching guide is structured as airway, breathing, circulation and depth, remembered as A-B-C-D, with respiratory rate, heart rate, peripheral pulse rate and quality, mucous membrane colour and capillary refill time, nerve reflexes, jaw tone and temperature recorded on a chart every two to five minutes, by a trained person whose only job is the anaesthetic. The technician's contribution is observation, recording and escalation within scope; the decision to change a drug or a vaporiser setting belongs to the veterinarian, and the anaesthetic chart is a legal record as well as a clinical one.
lessons.example: A fictional dog is in the operating theatre for an ovariohysterectomy, and you are the designated monitor. At 09:20 the dog is intubated, breathing spontaneously at a rate you count as twelve chest movements in thirty seconds, which is twenty-four breaths per minute, and you record twenty-four with the time and your initials. At 09:25 the surgeon clips the abdomen and the heart rate you are auscultating rises from 92 to 132, the respiratory rate rises, and the leg you are holding tenses. You do not read that as a problem with the anaesthetic machine. You read it as a response to a stimulus given before the incision, which is one of the most reliable depth signs there is, and you report it in the order the observations occurred: 09:25, clipping commenced, heart rate 92 to 132, respiratory rate rose, increased muscle tone noted. The veterinarian decides what to do about the depth of anaesthesia, and your record gives them the evidence. Compare that with a different situation an hour later. At 10:20 the surgeon asks for clamps on the ovarian pedicle, and this time the heart rate does not move, jaw tone remains loose, the corneal reflex is present but slow, and the respiratory rate has fallen to eighteen with shallower excursions on the reservoir bag. Nothing is dramatic, and yet the combination of a falling respiratory rate, a slack jaw and an unresponsive cardiovascular system points in the other direction from the first event, towards a plane that may be deeper than the surgeon wants. The single numbers in both episodes are uninteresting on their own. What carries information is the pairing of a known stimulus with a known response, recorded with times, so that the next observation can be compared with the last. Over a ninety minute anaesthetic, a chart filled in every five minutes yields eighteen data points and one filled in every two minutes yields forty-five; either discipline is workable, and a chart with irregular untimed entries is neither.
lessons.question: During maintenance of anaesthesia a technician observes that the horse on the table has developed nystagmus and a central eyeball position. Which interpretation is the safest starting point?
lessons.answer: In this species nystagmus can be caused by severe hypoxia or hypercapnia rather than a light plane of anaesthesia, so the finding should be reported as a possible ventilation and oxygenation problem rather than assumed to mean the patient is too lightly anaesthetised
lessons.distractor: Nystagmus always indicates excitement and a light plane of anaesthesia, so the finding means the patient needs more anaesthetic depth
lessons.correction: Nystagmus does usually accompany excitement and a light plane, which is exactly why the reflex-based reading is dangerous when it is applied without species knowledge. Veterinary teaching material states that dissociative agents such as ketamine produce nystagmus at moderate depth, and that in horses central stimulation from severe hypoxia or hypercapnia produces the same sign, in which case the patient is not too lightly anaesthetised but in danger. A central eyeball position is also normal in horses, unlike most other species. The safe response is to treat the finding as a signal to check oxygenation and ventilation and to escalate, not to conclude anything about depth on one sign.

depth.definitions: Depth of anaesthesia is the degree of central nervous system depression produced by an anaesthetic protocol, judged from several signs rather than one. Guedel's signs and stages are a historical classification of anaesthetic depth described for ether in cats, dividing anaesthesia into stages and planes. A nerve reflex here means a repeatable response such as the palpebral reflex, elicited by touching the eyelid, the corneal reflex, elicited by touching the cornea, and the pupillary light reflex. Jaw tone is the resistance felt when the jaw is gently opened, and medioventral eyeball rotation describes the eye turning downward and inward. The anaesthetic chart, or anaesthesia record, is the contemporaneous written account of parameters and interventions, taken at an interval and signed, which serves clinical and legal purposes. Scope of practice is the boundary of what a team member may decide alone; here recognition, recording and escalation belong to the technician, while changing the anaesthetic plan belongs to the veterinarian.
depth.mechanism: Why does a pattern beat a number? Every individual channel is confounded. Reflexes vary by species and are modified by the drug class given. Eye signs are altered by dissociatives. Heart rate can move in either direction with depth and also responds to surgical stimulus, to blood loss and to pain. The reason responses to stimulation rank highest in the reliability hierarchy is that they integrate the whole system: if a patient moves purposefully, reacts to clamping, or mounts a sudden cardiovascular or respiratory response to a stimulus that should now be non-painful, then whatever the drug concentrations are, the patient is not adequately covered at that moment. There is also a mechanical reason the pattern should be recorded rather than remembered. Depth changes with time and with the surgical phase, so a single assessment is a snapshot, while a chart with times and initials supports comparison and makes the clinical reasoning auditable after the event.
depth.secondExample: A fictional rabbit is anaesthetised for a dental procedure. Rabbits are a species in which a technician cannot rely on the same reflex hierarchy that works in a dog, and the published readings for this lesson address dogs, and in the Western University notes horses, rather than lagomorphs. The defensible behaviour is therefore humility plus structure. You record the parameters you can obtain reliably in this species, you note explicitly on the chart which signs were unobtainable and why, and you flag the patient as a species for which your team's monitoring protocol does not fully apply. Compare that with a fictional cat receiving a ketamine-containing protocol in which you see nystagmus at a depth that is clearly adequate for the procedure; here the species is familiar and the drug class explains the sign, so nystagmus is not read as light anaesthesia. The contrast between the two cases is the whole lesson: the same sign carries different meaning according to species and drug, and the discipline is to state which of the two you actually know.
depth.mistake: A common misconception is that a single sign, such as a missing palpebral reflex, proves that the patient is at surgical depth and can be used as a switch. Missing palpebral reflexes in dogs at an adequate plane are expected, so the sign is uninformative in the direction people want, and its absence in another species could mean the patient is too deep. A second misconception is that bradycardia in an anaesthetised patient always means the patient is too deep; heart rate is classified as a less reliable depth sign precisely because it moves for several reasons. The diagnostic correction is to ask, of every sign, three questions: which species, which drugs, and what has just happened to the patient? If a sign cannot be interpreted with those answers available, it should be recorded as a raw observation and escalated rather than converted into a conclusion.
depth.application: Nonblocking task, ten to fifteen minutes. Take a blank anaesthetic record or draw the columns yourself: time, respiratory rate with the counting method, heart rate, pulse quality, mucous membrane colour and capillary refill time, reflexes examined, jaw tone, temperature, and a final column headed events. Write an explicit rubric row for yourself before you begin: at least one entry every five minutes, every entry carries a time and your initials, every value states the method used, and every observation is separated from any interpretation. Then review your own blank form and note in one sentence which columns in your hospital are usually left empty. Self-review question: if a colleague read only your form, could they reconstruct what was normal for this patient, what changed, and when?
depth.summary: Depth of anaesthesia is a moving pattern assembled from reflexes, muscle tone, eye signs and, above all, responses to stimulation, read with species and drug class in mind and recorded against the clock. The classic staging system explains where the signs came from and why they no longer fit modern techniques, while the practical structure, airway, breathing, circulation and depth with monitoring at fixed intervals, is what survives. The transferable habit is to treat every single sign as ambiguous alone and every timed series of signs as informative, which is the same habit that will be used in the recovery lesson that follows and in every subsequent shift on the ward.

readings.title: Lyon Lee, Anesthetic Monitoring (Western University of Health Sciences, College of Veterinary Medicine teaching notes)
readings.note: Open PDF without a paywall. Read the table of Guedel's signs and stages, then the three lists headed most reliable, reliable and less reliable signs of anaesthetic depth, and the short paragraphs on the palpebral, corneal and nystagmus signs with their species and drug exceptions. visual.title: From one sign to a pattern: the channels a monitor reads at the same moment
visual.description: A labelled diagram with a single patient at the centre and four vertical channels around it, each channel showing what it contributes to the depth judgement and what makes it unreliable in isolation, converging at the bottom on one decision, report and record.
steps: Channel one, reflexes and eye signs: palpebral, corneal, pupillary light, nystagmus, lacrimation, eyeball position, each annotated with its species exception, such as the palpebral reflex in dogs and the central eyeball position in horses.

Channel two, muscle tone and spontaneous movement: jaw tone graded from tight to loose, plus any purposeful movement, swallowing or nystagmus, labelled as strongly informative when it occurs in response to a stimulus.

Channel three, responses to stimulation: clipping, surgical preparation, drape placement, clamp placement, incision, each with space to record heart rate, respiratory rate and blood pressure before and after the stimulus.

Channel four, the timed record: time, values, method, initials and events, at an interval of two to five minutes, with a branch arrow labelled escalate to the veterinarian for any unexplained change and no branch for a technician decision to alter the anaesthetic.

lessons.title: The monitoring toolkit: what each channel measures and how it misleads
lessons.explanation: Monitors extend the senses, and every one of them measures something narrower than a technician may assume, which is why they are read alongside hands, eyes and ears rather than instead of them. The American College of Veterinary Anesthesia and Analgesia revised its small animal monitoring guidelines in 2025, the first major revision since 2009, developed with the North American Veterinary Anesthesia Society and the Academy of Veterinary Technicians in Anesthesia and Analgesia. The published summary of that revision lists updates in hemodynamic, respiratory and thermoregulatory monitoring, expanded recommendations for neuromuscular blockade monitoring, enhanced personnel protocols and detailed record-keeping practices including safety checklists, and it deliberately organises its recommendations into basic, advanced and alternative tiers so that clinics with different resources can see what a minimum standard looks like and what extra equipment adds. That tiering is itself a lesson in evidence: a guideline that names a basic tier is admitting that the technology is not the point. What the channels actually measure is worth stating plainly. Pulse oximetry estimates the percentage of haemoglobin saturated with oxygen from the absorption of light through tissue; it says nothing directly about ventilation or blood pressure. Capnography measures the concentration or partial pressure of carbon dioxide in expired gas and therefore carries information about both ventilation and, through the shape of the waveform, about circulation and equipment function, which is why a review written for veterinary practice notes that anaesthetic agents commonly cause respiratory depression leading to hypoventilation and hypercapnia, and that waveform familiarity supports early detection of complications. Blood pressure devices, whether Doppler or oscillometric, estimate arterial pressure and are read with cuff size and position in mind. Electrocardiography shows rhythm rather than the adequacy of circulation, which is why the AAHA anaesthesia guidelines describe monitoring rhythm by auscultation, electrocardiography or by noting pulse to heart rate incongruity with Doppler or an SpO2 waveform. Neuromuscular blockade monitoring is a separate channel again, and the 2025 revision is reported to push for objective assessment of block rather than reliance on subjective signs such as spontaneous breathing, because residual paralysis matters at extubation. Every one of these instruments can fail in a way that looks like a patient problem. A pulse oximeter probe placed on a poorly perfused site, a probe on pigmented or hair-covered skin, motion, ambient light and a leaking anaesthetic circuit all generate numbers and waveforms that look authoritative. The technician's job is to ask of every trace whether it matches the patient in front of them: is the pulse rate on the monitor the same as the rate counted over the heart, is the waveform plausibly the animal's own, does the reading move when the probe is repositioned, and is the patient's colour consistent with the number on the screen? Discrepancy is a finding in its own right and it is escalated. Deciding to change a machine setting, to change a drug, or to accept a number as clinically satisfactory is a veterinarian's decision.
lessons.example: A fictional cat is anaesthetised, and the pulse oximeter reads ninety-five per cent. The temptation is to treat that number as a fact about arterial oxygen. The published study of pulse oximetry accuracy in llamas and alpacas is a useful reminder of what the number contains, and it applies the same measurement principle that veterinary oximeters use in cats and dogs: when the investigators compared the saturation estimated by the oximeter with the saturation measured from arterial blood, the oximeter reading was consistently between zero and six percentage points different, with a bias of about minus two point six points. On average the device understated arterial saturation, so a displayed reading of ninety-five corresponds to an arterial saturation of roughly ninety-seven and a half per cent, though individual readings spread across a range and the direction of the error can reverse. In the same study, whether a reading could be obtained at all depended enormously on where the probe was placed: attempts on the tongue and nasal septum succeeded about ninety-seven per cent of the time, the lip about eighty per cent, the vulva about sixty-two per cent, the prepuce about fifty-nine per cent, and the ear and scrotum under fifty per cent. Now return to the cat. The displayed value is ninety-five, the probe is on a shaved ear, and the cat has just been repositioned. A monitor-only reading would say oxygenation is acceptable. A technician reading the whole picture says something different: the reading is ninety-five on a site the study suggests is unreliable, the patient was just moved, and the probe must be repositioned and the reading rechecked against the patient's mucous membrane colour before any conclusion is recorded. Nothing in that reasoning required a decision about the anaesthetic; the reasoning required deciding whether the instrument was telling the truth.
lessons.question: A patient's capnograph shows a falling end-tidal carbon dioxide value while a second patient's pulse oximeter shows a reading obtained from a probe you know is poorly positioned. Which of the following best describes how these two instrument findings should be handled?
lessons.answer: Both should be treated as provisional until the underlying measurement is confirmed, because the capnograph reflects exhaled carbon dioxide and can signal changed ventilation as well as equipment or sampling problems, while the oximeter reading is known to depend heavily on probe site and contact, so each finding is verified against the patient and reported rather than accepted or dismissed
lessons.distractor: The capnograph is a ventilation monitor so its value should be accepted and reported immediately, while a poorly positioned oximeter probe can simply be ignored because a wrong site makes the reading meaningless
lessons.correction: Discarding an oximetry reading because the site is doubtful throws away a useful observation, namely that the reading cannot be trusted and the site needs changing. Accepting a capnography value without checking the patient and the sampling path does the opposite, converting a possibly technical artefact into a clinical claim. Both errors come from the same source, treating a monitor as an answer rather than as one measurement channel with known failure modes. The disciplined response is identical in both cases: check the patient, check the device, then report the finding and what you did about it.

depth.definitions: Pulse oximetry estimates arterial haemoglobin oxygen saturation from light absorption through a pulsating tissue bed. Capnography measures the concentration or partial pressure of carbon dioxide in expired gas and displays a waveform over time, with the end-tidal value taken at the end of expiration. Hypoventilation means inadequate alveolar ventilation and is reflected as rising exhaled carbon dioxide; hypercapnia is an excess of carbon dioxide in the blood. A Doppler blood pressure device uses ultrasound to detect flow and detects the return of flow as a cuff is deflated, while an oscillometric device detects pressure oscillations in the cuff. Electrocardiography records electrical cardiac activity, that is rhythm, not cardiac output. Neuromuscular blockade monitoring assesses the degree of paralysis produced by blocking agents. A monitoring tier means a ranked set of recommendations for different resource levels.
depth.mechanism: Consider why these channels are complementary rather than competitive. Oxygenation and ventilation are different physiological jobs: a patient can breathe a normal volume of gas and still be poorly oxygenated if gas exchange in the lung is impaired, and a patient can have well-oxygenated arterial blood while retaining carbon dioxide because ventilation is inadequate. If that distinction is understood, then it follows that a normal oximetry reading cannot reassure anyone about ventilation, and a normal capnography value cannot reassure anyone about oxygenation. The same reasoning explains why rhythm and pressure tell different stories: a heart can generate an orderly electrical pattern and still move very little blood, so electrocardiography and a pulse check are not redundant. This is why the published guidance recommends recording several channels and examining them together, and why the technician's contribution is a description of which channel is currently trustworthy.
depth.secondExample: A fictional clinic has no capnograph and relies on a stethoscope, a Doppler and hands. Rather than treating this as a gap that invalidates monitoring, the 2025 guideline structure is used as intended: the basic tier is the floor. The team writes a protocol that specifies, for each patient, which parameters are recorded, at what interval, by whom and on what form, and which findings trigger an escalation. The protocol also states what the clinic cannot measure and what the technician should therefore document as unavailable rather than guess. Compare that with a fictional practice that has an advanced monitor and no dedicated person to watch it, where alarms sound in an empty room and the chart is completed at the end of the case from memory. The equipment advantage is real in the first practice and notional in the second, because the guideline's own framing treats a trained dedicated observer as the load-bearing element and the machine as an extension of them.
depth.mistake: The most expensive misconception is that an instrument reading settles a question. A technician who writes that the patient is fine because the saturation reads ninety-eight has recorded a machine output as a clinical judgement and skipped the patient. A closely related error is silence: noticing that a reading does not match the patient and saying nothing because the number on the screen looks acceptable. The diagnostic correction is to force the comparison every time, in this order. Look at the patient, look at the monitor, and ask whether the two agree. If they do not agree, state the disagreement out loud with a time attached. If they do agree, record both. What must never be recorded is a monitor value presented as a conclusion about the patient's wellbeing.
depth.application: Nonblocking task, fifteen minutes. Using your own hospital's monitors or a labelled photograph of them, write a one-page table with one row per device you can access: what it measures, an example of what it cannot tell you on its own, and one failure mode you could recognise without any change in the patient. Then add a column titled could I confirm this another way, and fill it with a second channel, such as a palpated pulse to check a displayed rate, or mucous membrane colour to check an oxygen saturation. Self-review rubric: you can name a second channel for every device, and at least one row ends with the words report to the veterinarian rather than a number.
depth.summary: Every monitoring device measures one narrow thing and fails in characteristic ways, so the technician's skill is not interpreting a screen but testing whether the screen agrees with the patient. The 2025 change to the anaesthesia monitoring guidelines, with its basic, advanced and alternative tiers and its emphasis on objective neuromuscular blockade assessment, personnel protocols and record keeping, demonstrates that the guideline authors themselves treat trained observation as the foundation. Knowing what each channel does and does not measure is what allows a technician to escalate the interesting event, which is the disagreement between a device and a patient, rather than the reassuring number that may have been produced by an artefact.

readings.title: American College of Veterinary Anesthesia and Analgesia, Updated ACVAA Small Animal Anesthesia Monitoring Guidelines Are Available (2025)
readings.note: Short open announcement page. Read the first three paragraphs, which list what the 2025 revision changed, namely hemodynamic, respiratory and thermoregulatory monitoring, neuromuscular blockade monitoring, personnel protocols, record keeping and checklists, and the sentence explaining that basic, advanced and alternative recommendations are included to cover different clinical settings. Use it to see how a professional college ranks recommendations when resources differ, then follow the link on that page to the open access guideline if your institution has access.

readings.title: Sarah Shippy, Capnography: Assessing Ventilation During Anesthesia (Today's Veterinary Practice, 2024)
readings.note: Open clinical review written for practice teams. Read the abstract and take-home points on why anaesthetic agents cause respiratory depression, hypoventilation, hypercapnia and potentially hypoxemia, then the section on waveforms and the troubleshooting discussion of complications associated with expired carbon dioxide. Section-specific direction: use the waveform discussion to learn the difference between a value that is low, a value that is high and a waveform that is distorted, because those three problems have different causes. Educational review, not a protocol.

readings.title: Pulse oximetry in camelids: assessment of clinical application of pulse oximetry probes (Veterinary Medicine and Science, open access)
readings.note: Free full text on PMC. Read the abstract and the results for the two study parts: the comparison of oximeter saturation with arterial saturation measured by co-oximetry, and the reported success rates by probe site, tongue and nasal septum, lip, vulva, prepuce, ear and scrotum. This is the source of the bias and site figures cited in the lesson. The subjects are llamas and alpacas, so transfer the measurement principle, not the specific numbers, to cats and dogs.

visual.title: Four channels, four failure modes, one verification habit
visual.description: A two row diagram. The top row shows four devices, oximeter, capnograph, blood pressure device and electrocardiograph, each labelled with what it measures. The bottom row shows the same four devices with a matched artefact or limitation, and an arrow from each to a single box in the centre labelled confirm on the patient and on a second channel.
steps: Top row, what each channel measures: oximeter, arterial haemoglobin oxygen saturation; capnograph, expired carbon dioxide concentration and waveform shape, hence ventilation and some circulatory information; blood pressure device, estimated arterial pressure with cuff size and position as conditions; electrocardiograph, cardiac rhythm, not the adequacy of circulation.

Bottom row, matched failure modes: oximeter, poor probe site, poor perfusion, pigment, motion or ambient light; capnograph, sampling problems, circuit leak or seal issues and the need to read the waveform and not only the number; blood pressure device, cuff size, cuff position and a pulse to heart rate mismatch; electrocardiograph, an orderly rhythm with weak or absent pulses.

Centre box, the verification habit: name the channel being doubted, name the second channel used to check it, and name the finding that would change your mind, for example a palpated pulse that does not match the displayed rate.
Bottom line, the escalation and no decision zone: every unresolved disagreement is reported with a time, and the diagram carries no branch in which a technician changes the anaesthetic plan.

lessons.title: Pain scoring in patients that conceal pain: matching the tool to the question
lessons.explanation: Pain scoring moves past the question of whether a patient looks painful to the more useful question of which instrument answers which clinical question, and what its published limitations are. The 2022 AAHA Pain Management Guidelines for Dogs and Cats build their assessment section around reproducibility rather than intuition, and they publish a table that classifies each tool by whether it targets acute or chronic pain, who may use it, how easy it is to use, what it is for, and how well validated it is. That table is unusually honest, and reading it is the core skill of this lesson. For acute feline pain, the Feline Grimace Scale is listed as simple and validated, suitable for screening and monitoring, and it was developed for naturally occurring acute pain with a published cut-off that indicates when analgesic intervention should be considered. The UNESP-Botucatu multidimensional composite pain scale is listed as valid but moderately demanding to use, and the Glasgow Composite Measure Pain Scale for cats as moderately validated, while the Colorado Acute Pain Scale for felines is listed as simple but not validated. In dogs, the widely used instruments include the Colorado State University Canine Acute Pain Scale and the Glasgow short-form Composite Measure Pain Scale, and the guidelines describe scores being tracked over time rather than read once. For chronic pain the tools change hands: the guidelines list owner-completed instruments such as the Musculoskeletal Pain Screening Checklist, the Feline Musculoskeletal Pain Index, the Canine Brief Pain Inventory with its eleven questions, the twenty-three question Liverpool Osteoarthritis in Dogs and the Sleep and Nighttime Restlessness Evaluation questionnaire, and they state that no owner-completed instrument has been developed for acute pain, so at-home acute assessment must be guided by the veterinary team. Why does concealment matter so much at the front end? The guidelines describe cats as mid-level predators that exhibit both predatory and prey-type behaviour, which shapes what an observer will and will not see: a cat may not overtly express pain, yet it does produce detectable signs. Concealment is not the same as absence, and it means the untrained glance systematically underestimates. The practical consequence is a division of labour. The technician contributes structured observation, correct use of the tool the practice has chosen, a score recorded with a time, and the follow-up score after an intervention, because responsiveness, the ability of a scale to detect clinically important change, is one of the properties that makes a scale useful. Deciding whether and what to give for pain belongs to the veterinarian, and the guidelines themselves are explicit that neither analgesics nor thresholds are for untrained application. A technician who feels a number in the record and a behaviour at the cage side disagreeing should say so; the disagreement is data.
lessons.example: A fictional cat is admitted the evening after an abdominal procedure. At 22:00 a colleague glances in, sees the cat lying still with its eyes closed, and writes comfortable in the record. At 23:00 you perform the structured assessment your practice has chosen for cats. You observe from outside the cage before opening it, you note head position, ear orientation and facial tension, then you interact gently and notice that the cat does not turn its head towards you, does not groom, has left the food untouched and has a tense abdominal posture. You record the elements separately, then the resulting score with the time and your initials, using the practice's chosen form so that the next shift can score identically. Two things happened that did not happen at 22:00. The first is that the observation was broken into components, which is what makes a grimace-based or composite tool repeatable between people, instead of one global impression. The second is that the record now contains a baseline, so that when the score is repeated after an intervention the team can see change rather than a snapshot. Now take the contrast. A fictional dog in the next cage wags its tail, greets every person who walks past, and has done so since admission. A technician who treats friendliness as proof of comfort has misread the instrument, because the guidelines note that owners know their dog's normal behaviour and that deviations from it suggest pain; a dog that is unusually clingy, or suddenly still, or not settling, may be showing a change in behaviour rather than a comfortable state. In both cages the defensible output is the same: components observed, score with time and initials, baseline established, change reported, and no drug decision made by the technician.
lessons.question: A practice uses one generic pain scale with no facial expression components for every species it treats, applied once on admission. Which statement best identifies why this is a weak assessment system even though the staff record a score conscientiously?
lessons.answer: Pain tools are species-specific and differ in what they are validated to detect, and the published guidance expects scores to be repeated so that change and response to intervention can be seen, so a single cross-species score on admission produces a number with neither the right content nor a comparison
lessons.distractor: The system is weak only because the staff have not been trained, since any pain scale produces correct results in any species once the user is competent
lessons.correction: Training helps, but it cannot repair a tool that was not designed for the species or the question. Grimace-based assessment was developed separately for cats and for other species precisely because the facial features associated with pain differ, and the guideline table rates instruments differently for validity and for purpose. Adding to that, a single admission score has no comparator, so it can neither detect worsening nor demonstrate improvement. The correction is not to abandon scoring, which would return the team to unstructured impressions, but to select species-appropriate instruments, use them consistently, record the components next to the score, and repeat them at defined intervals.

depth.definitions: A pain assessment instrument is a structured set of observable items, each scored, which produces a total that can be compared over time. Validity is the property of measuring what it claims to measure; reliability is the reproducibility of the result between and within observers; responsiveness is the ability to detect clinically important change; an intervention threshold, or cut-off, is the score at or above which analgesic treatment should be considered. A composite scale combines several domains, such as posture, activity and response to palpation, while a grimace scale uses facial action units, such as ear position and orbital tightening, rated as absent, partially present or markedly present. Acute pain is pain of recent onset, typically after surgery or injury, while chronic pain persists, and osteoarthritis is the most common chronic cause in cats. Owner-completed instruments are questionnaires a client fills in, and they exist for chronic pain but not for acute pain.
depth.mechanism: Why does reproduction replace impression? Because a single observer's global judgement embeds their memory of other patients, their assumptions about the species and, in cats, their expectation that a quiet animal is a comfortable one. A structured tool forces the observer to look at named features in a fixed order and to separate what they see from what they conclude, which is what makes comparison between two observers possible at all. The second mechanism is the sedative and anaesthetic effect that the guidelines acknowledge: drugs alter demeanour and responsiveness, so a score taken while a patient is still under the influence of an anaesthetic agent is not a clean measurement of pain. That is why the same patient needs to be scored again later, and it is why a technician should record which drugs have been given and when, alongside the score, so that the score is interpreted rather than merely accumulated.
depth.secondExample: A fictional rabbit is hospitalised after a dental procedure, and the practice has no species-specific tool for rabbits. Two responses are possible. The first is to borrow the cat form, apply it to the rabbit, and record a number that looks scientific and is not validated for the species. The second is to record the components that a rabbit does show, such as posture, hunched position, coat condition, eye appearance and food intake, state explicitly on the record that the practice has no validated instrument for this species and that the observation is structured but unvalidated, and ask the veterinarian whether a species-appropriate tool is available. The second response is more useful to the patient precisely because it does not pretend to a precision that the tool cannot supply, and it hands the veterinarian a clear picture of what was observed. Contrast that with the fictional cat where a validated tool is available: there, the scale should be used as published, including its published threshold, and the decision at the threshold is the veterinarian's.
depth.mistake: The persistent misconception is that a low pain score means the patient is comfortable. In cats especially, it can mean only that the chosen instrument was wrong for the species, that the observer relied on the absence of vocalisation, or that the score was taken at a moment when the patient was heavily sedated. A second misconception is that paleness of response proves stoicism rather than pain. The diagnostic correction is to check the instrument before trusting the result: is this tool listed as validated for this species, for this type of pain, and for this kind of observer? If any answer is no, the score must be recorded as structured observation, with the limitation written beside it, and the patient should be reassessed after the drugs have had time to wear off and after any intervention, so that responsiveness is being measured rather than a single mood.
depth.application: Nonblocking task, twenty minutes. Find the pain assessment tools your own practice actually uses, one for dogs and one for cats if both exist. On one page write: the exact name of each tool, whether it targets acute or chronic pain, who completes it, and what its published validation claim is if you can find it. Then write the reassessment interval your practice uses, or state that none is defined. Self-review rubric: you can name the species each tool is for, you can state one documented limitation, and you have written down the interval at which you would repeat the score. Model response for a practice with no tools: an accurate statement that no validated instrument is in use, followed by a request to the veterinarian and the head nurse, not an improvised scale.
depth.summary: Pain scoring is a matched-methods problem. Species determine which facial and behavioural features carry information, the clinical question determines whether an acute or chronic instrument is right, and validity determines how much weight the resulting number deserves. Cats and prey-type patients express pain in ways a casual glance systematically under-detects, which is precisely why the guidelines invest in structured, reproducible, repeatable tools and in owner knowledge of normal behaviour. The technician's durable contribution is the disciplined use of the right instrument, the component-level record, the timed baseline and the repeat score after intervention, with every treatment decision left where it belongs, with the veterinarian.

lessons.title: The recovery period: airway, temperature and the first hours after extubation
lessons.explanation: Recovery is the phase in which the anaesthetic that was so carefully titrated is withdrawn, and it is the phase in which the published data locate most anaesthetic deaths in small animals, with the first three hours after surgery identified as the period of greatest risk. The 2020 AAHA Anesthesia and Monitoring Guidelines treat recovery as the fourth phase of a continuum rather than as the moment anaesthesia stops mattering, and the University of Edinburgh monitoring guide states the same principle from the teaching side: monitoring starts at induction and continues until the patient is conscious in recovery, because an anaesthetised patient cannot protect its airway or regulate its own temperature. Three mechanisms dominate the recovery room. The first is the airway. Extubation is a decision with criteria, not a convenience. The AAHA guidelines state that the patient should be extubated when the respiratory rate and oxygen saturation are within normal limits and the patient can adequately protect its airway by vigorously swallowing; the cuff is deflated immediately before the tube is removed, and intravenous access is kept until the patient is extubated and in sternal recumbency with physiological parameters back to normal. For patients that have had a dental procedure or rhinoscopy the guidelines suggest positioning the nose slightly lower than the back of the head and leaving the cuff slightly inflated during extubation, so that blood and fluid drain out rather than into the airway. A patient with a partially functional airway makes noise, and an absent noise in a patient that was noisy a moment ago is equally informative. The second mechanism is temperature. Hypothermia is described in the guidelines as able to cause multiple physiological complications, including delayed drug metabolism, which prolongs recovery further, so warming devices are recommended throughout the recovery phase, and the guidelines note that drugs change the arithmetic of heat loss: alpha-2 agonists cause peripheral vasoconstriction while inhalant agents cause vasodilation, so the same room and the same blanket do not produce the same effect in every patient. The third mechanism is metabolic. The guidelines warn that hypoglycemia, particularly in small or neonatal patients, can prolong recovery, and they recommend monitoring blood glucose frequently in those patients. Two supporting rules are easy to forget and matter in a busy hospital. Someone responsible must remain with the patient; the ACVAA standard quoted in a recent review is that a responsible person must remain with the patient, even if not focused solely on anaesthesia, whereas human anaesthesia guidelines require constant monitoring by a physician or a supervised assistant, and the review notes that the difference between the two standards is one plausible reason for the higher perianesthetic death rate in veterinary species. And documentation continues: the AAHA guidelines list support and monitoring in recovery, and documentation of patient parameters during anaesthesia and recovery, as parts of the plan. The technician's role in all of this is to know the discharge criteria, apply them by observation, keep the patient warm and monitored, and escalate any patient who is not waking, is not swallowing, is bleeding, is shivering, or whose behaviour at home might later suggest a problem the hospital never saw.
lessons.example: A fictional dog is extubated at 11:40 after a one hundred minute procedure. At 11:42 the dog swallows, lifts its head, and looks around; the respiratory rate is within normal limits for the patient and the oxygen saturation reading is acceptable, so the extubation criteria are met, the cuff was deflated before the tube came out, and the dog is positioned in sternal recumbency with the head supported. The intravenous catheter stays in place until parameters are normal and the patient is sternal, because access may be needed again. The warm air blanket that was started before induction stays on. At 11:55 the dog shivers, the rectal temperature is recorded at thirty-six point two degrees Celsius, and the record shows that temperature was thirty-eight point one before induction. Nothing about that number requires a technician to reason about drugs; it requires the technician to recognise the trend, keep warming the patient, check blood glucose if the hospital protocol calls for it in this patient, and report the finding with its time. Over the next ninety minutes the temperature is recorded every fifteen minutes, which is six data points, and the trend is now falling then rising rather than one isolated value. Contrast that with a fictional cat aged nineteen years and weighing a small fraction of the dog, recovering from a dental with blood-stained fluid in its mouth. Here the extubation order specifically matters: extubating with the nose positioned lower than the back of the head and the cuff still slightly inflated reduces the chance that fluid in the mouth runs into the airway, and the guidelines' warning about hypoglycemia in small and neonatal patients means blood glucose is checked rather than assumed. In both patients the technician's output is the same shape: criteria checked, the reason recorded, the numbers recorded with times, warmth provided, and any failure to meet a criterion reported immediately. What the technician does not do is decide to remove a tube early because the room needs turning around, or to re-dose anaesthetic because the patient is noisy.
lessons.question: A patient has been extubated and is in sternal recumbency but remains dull, is not swallowing, and has a dropping temperature. Which response best reflects recovery-phase practice as published?
lessons.answer: Treat the failure to meet the extubation and recovery criteria and the falling temperature as findings to report and manage within the protocol, keeping the patient on continuous observation, continuing active warming, continuing to monitor parameters and documenting each value with a time, because hypothermia and other causes of delayed recovery require veterinary evaluation
lessons.distractor: Accept the state as normal emergence and simply continue warming the patient, since gentle drowsiness and a low temperature are expected after anaesthesia and require no escalation as long as the patient is breathing
lessons.correction: Drowsiness after anaesthesia is expected; a patient that cannot protect its airway and whose temperature is falling is not simply drowsy. The published guidance links hypothermia to delayed drug metabolism and hence to prolonged recovery, lists the first hours after surgery as the period of greatest anaesthetic risk, and requires a responsible person to remain with the patient with parameters documented through recovery. Deferring to expectation, in the form of the phrase this is normal after anaesthesia, is the specific error that recovery rooms make, because it converts an unexplained observation into a category and stops the escalation clock.

depth.definitions: Recovery is the phase from the end of anaesthetic maintenance until the patient is conscious and physiologically stable. Extubation is removal of the endotracheal tube, and the cuff is the small balloon that seals the tube against the trachea and must be deflated before removal. Sternal recumbency means lying on the chest, which supports ventilation and airway protection better than lateral or dorsal recumbency in a waking patient. Hypothermia is a core temperature below the normal range and is a common complication of small animal anaesthesia. Peripheral vasoconstriction is narrowing of skin blood vessels, which reduces heat loss to the environment, while vasodilation is widening, which increases it. Hypoglycemia is low blood glucose. A discharge criterion here means a documented standard the patient must meet before a phase is considered complete, not a legal discharge from hospital.
depth.mechanism: The reason recovery deserves separate teaching rather than being treated as the tail of the operation is that the patient's physiology is moving in a direction the anaesthetist did not fully intend. Drug concentrations are falling, so protective reflexes return at different rates in different systems, and a patient can be awake enough to raise its head while still unable to swallow safely. Thermoregulation returns last in many patients, and the recovery room is often the coldest room in the building because doors are opening constantly. Heat loss continues while heat production is depressed, so a temperature that is merely low at extubation can become a temperature that is dangerous twenty minutes later, and the depressed metabolism that accompanies hypothermia slows the clearance of drugs, which lengthens the very period of risk. The same feedback loop explains why recovery monitoring is a documentation task and not a glance: the trend is the clinical finding, and a trend requires a series.
depth.secondExample: A fictional brachycephalic dog recovers from a skin procedure. Airway anatomy already makes inspiration harder, and a partially obstructed airway after extubation may present as increased effort, a changed noise or decreasing tolerance of recumbency rather than as an obvious emergency. The relevant discipline is to keep the patient under the same scheduled observations as any other recovery patient and to escalate a change early, because the airway is the first letter of the A-B-C-D monitoring structure precisely because it fails fastest. Compare that with a fictional patient recovering after an abdominal procedure with a light bandage, where the same observations apply but the likely early abnormality is different, such as a swelling or a dressing that has become soiled. In both cases the technician is checking named things on a schedule, and in neither case is the technician deciding whether the patient's anatomy or surgery explains the finding. The contrast shows that recovery monitoring is a fixed set of observations applied to patients with very different vulnerabilities, and that the flexibility is in the escalation, not in whether the observations happen.
depth.mistake: The commonest recovery-room error is extubating on a timetable rather than on criteria, because the patient looks ready or the next case is waiting, which risks removing the tube from a patient that still cannot protect its airway. A second error is treating warmth as comfort rather than as treatment, so warming is stopped once the patient stops shivering, when shivering is itself a sign that heat is being lost faster than it is produced. A third is the undocumented recovery: numbers reviewed from memory later. The diagnostic correction is to keep the extubation criteria visible at the recovery station, in writing, as the AAHA guidelines' emphasis on checklists implies, and to record temperature and other parameters at a stated interval so that any fall or rise is visible on paper before it is visible in the patient.
depth.application: Nonblocking task, fifteen minutes. Write the recovery checklist your practice would use, based on published criteria rather than memory. It should contain at least: the extubation criteria the patient must meet, the positioning used for patients with oral or nasal procedures, the temperature monitoring interval and warming method, the patients in whom blood glucose is monitored and how often, the interval for recording heart rate, respiratory rate and perfusion parameters, and the named person responsible for remaining with the patient. Then add two lines at the bottom: the findings that require immediate escalation, and a reminder that changes in anaesthetic or analgesic plan are veterinary decisions. Self-review rubric: every item on your list is an observation or a report, and no item is a dose, a drug choice or a change to a machine setting.
depth.summary: Recovery is a monitored phase with defined criteria, an airway at the top of the risk list, an active warming plan and specific metabolic traps in small and young patients, and it takes place in the hours in which published data place most veterinary anaesthetic deaths. The technician's contribution is criteria-based judgement about observation and escalation, not about drugs: checking that a patient can protect its own airway before the tube is removed, watching the trend in temperature rather than a single value, keeping the patient under a named person's care, and recording each parameter so that the next observer inherits evidence rather than opinion. The same habits transfer directly to the ward lesson that follows, where the patient is awake but still hospitalised and still at risk.

visual.title: Recovery as a sequence of gates the patient must pass
visual.description: A left to right flow diagram with four gates. lessons.title: Post-operative complications: describing what you see so someone else can act
lessons.explanation: Post-operative complications are where the technician's documentation habit meets clinical consequence, because the useful output is almost never a diagnosis; it is a serial description precise enough for a veterinarian to act on. The published literature makes one point clear before any list is attempted: complication rates are properties of particular populations and particular clinics, not of patients. A multicentre retrospective study of one hundred and eighty dogs undergoing intestinal resection and anastomosis recorded dehiscence in twelve of ninety-three sutured anastomoses, which is thirteen per cent, and four of eighty-seven stapled anastomoses, which is five per cent, and reported that dehiscence rates varied significantly among the participating clinics while no other variable was significantly associated with risk. The same lesson appears in the opposite direction in another study: a review of two hundred and twelve dogs and cats after surgical gastrotomy found confirmed dehiscence in two animals, which is about zero point nine four per cent, and concluded that the single-centre rate was lower than rates previously reported for the small intestine and that the event was too rare to analyse risk factors. Those two papers together teach something specific. A rate quoted as a percentage describes a cohort after the fact and cannot be used to predict what will happen to the patient in front of you, and the fact that the same complication varies by clinic and by procedure means that the clinic's own detection and recording practices are part of the measurement. Now consider what a technician can actually observe. Bleeding may appear as swelling at the site, bruising spreading beyond it, or a dressing that has become wet, and it also appears systemically as tachycardia, pallor, or a patient that becomes quieter and less responsive; the wound and the patient must be read together. Dehiscence, separation of a closed incision, may present as a gap, as a discharge, as suture material visible, or as a frank evisceration, and its management needs a specific conditioned reflex: do not push tissue back, do not handle exposed organ, cover the area with a sterile dressing moistened with a suitable solution as instructed by the veterinarian, keep the patient calm and warm, and escalate immediately and without delay, because this is time-critical. Swelling is another observation that becomes useful only with a comparator: a seroma, an accumulation of fluid under the skin, and a surgical site infection may look similar at one moment, so what helps is a recorded size, a described character, a temperature, and a note of whether the patient resents palpation. The same reasoning applies to the incision line for several days after discharge, which is why the owner is given explicit instructions about what to look at and what to report. Surgical site infection surveillance is treated as a formal activity in infection-control guidelines, with audits and identified infection rates used to detect trends, which is another reminder that the raw material for all of it is a technician's timed, factual entry rather than an impression. Finally, the technician observes the patient's comfort, appetite, urination and demeanour, and nausea, restlessness or unexplained vocalisation may be pain, may be dysphoria, and may be something else; the note should record the behaviour and the context, and the interpretation and any treatment is the veterinarian's.
lessons.example: A fictional cat returns to the ward after a laparotomy. At 16:00, on arrival from recovery, you record a full baseline: incision line described as clean and dry, mild swelling of the subcutaneous tissues noted with its approximate extent, the cat's temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate, mucous membrane colour, and the fact that the cat resents gentle palpation near the wound. That baseline is the single most valuable entry in the record, because every later entry will be a comparison against it. At 18:00 you repeat the observation. The described area of swelling has doubled, the dressing has a small fresh reddish mark at one corner, the cat's heart rate is higher than at 16:00 and its mucous membranes look paler to you than they did. You do not write that the cat is bleeding internally. You write what you saw, in order, with times, plus the fact that the finding is a change from your own baseline. A veterinarian reads that and decides what to do and how fast. Now consider a second patient, a dog sent home two days earlier with a skin incision after removal of a lump. The owner telephones because the wound looks different, and the technician's task is to ask structured questions rather than guess: is there a gap, is there discharge and what colour, is the area hot to touch, is the dog eating, is it licking the wound, and is there any bleeding. The answers are recorded and passed on. Compare the two situations and notice that the technique is identical: fix a baseline, describe in observable terms, note change over time, and route the interpretation to the person with the authority to make it. Notice also what the two published dehiscence studies do not license. Neither allows a technician to reassure an owner by quoting a percentage, because the percentage belongs to a study population and the owner's animal is an individual with its own wound, its own procedure and its own clinic's detection practices.
lessons.question: A technician notices that a patient's incision has a fresh gap with a small loop of tissue visible three days after surgery. Which action sequence is correct?
lessons.answer: Leave the tissue undisturbed, cover the area with a sterile dressing moistened as the veterinarian instructs, keep the patient calm, warm and under direct observation, and escalate immediately so the veterinarian sees the patient without delay
lessons.distractor: Clean the exposed tissue, attempt to replace it into the wound, and reapply a fresh bandage yourself before informing the veterinarian at the next medication round, since wound care is part of the technician's routine nursing duties
lessons.correction: Dehiscence with exposed tissue is time-critical, and attempting to replace the tissue risks further damage and contamination, so the correct technician action is protection and immediate escalation rather than an intervention. The misconception confuses the routine nature of dressing changes with the urgency of a surgical emergency: routine bandaging skills do not extend to handling exposed viscera. The technician's contribution is precise description, immediate protection and a fast, specific report, and the decision about what happens next belongs to the veterinarian.

depth.definitions: Dehiscence is separation of the layers of a closed surgical wound, ranging from a superficial gap to complete disruption with exposed deeper tissue or organs. Evisceration is the protrusion of organs through a wound. A seroma is a collection of serum in the tissue under a closed incision. Surgical site infection is an infection arising at the site of a surgical procedure and is tracked through surveillance in infection-control programmes. Dysphoria is a state of altered mental or behavioural state, distinguished here from pain because the two can look similar and have different implications. A baseline is the first documented observation against which later observations are compared. Odds ratio is a measure of association in a study, not a predictor for an individual patient.
depth.mechanism: Why is description more valuable than naming a condition? Because the treatment a wound needs depends on information the technician has and the diagnosis depends on information and authority the technician does not. A surgeon reading a note that says the swelling increased, the dressing has fresh blood at one corner, the heart rate rose and the mucous membranes are paler has everything needed to decide whether to open the wound, to re-dress it, to run blood work or to take the patient back to theatre. A surgeon reading a note that says the patient is bleeding internally has to determine what was seen before they can decide anything, and if the guess was wrong they must also discount it. Deterioration in complication studies is also a rate, not a prophecy, so the second reason to describe rather than predict is that prediction requires a base rate for an individual that does not exist; what does exist is the intra-patient comparison, which is available if and only if the earlier observations were recorded properly.
depth.secondExample: A fictional practice wants to reduce surgical site infections and starts counting them, as infection-control guidance recommends. Initially the count is useless, because the practice records wounds in free text and nobody can tell a seroma from an infection from a note. The team therefore writes a short structured wound entry: size, character of any swelling, presence of discharge and its appearance, whether the patient resents palpation, and the patient's temperature, each recorded at least once per shift and always at discharge with a photograph taken in a standard way. Months later the practice has something to review, because the entries are comparable. Compare that with a fictional practice that only writes appeared fine, and, when a wound later breaks down at home, has no way of knowing whether anything was different in the hospital. The same contrast, between a record that supports comparison and a record of reassurance, is the reason the two cited studies can report complication rates at all and the reason the clinic-to-clinic variation they found is a finding rather than noise.
depth.mistake: The most consequential error is resolution by reassurance: writing that the wound looks fine because the alternative is to escalate, or because the patient is not the technician's case. A second is intervening beyond scope, for example attempting to replace protruding tissue, cleaning an open wound with something not prescribed, or reapplying a bandage when the correct action was to call for help. A third is recording a diagnosis instead of an observation, which quietly deletes the evidence. The diagnostic correction is a mental checklist for every patient on the ward: what was the baseline, what is different now, can I describe it without naming a disease, and who needs to know and how fast? If the description cannot be produced, the observation is not yet complete.
depth.application: Nonblocking task, twenty minutes. Design the wound entry your practice would use for every surgical patient, on one page and in your own words. Include: the timing of the baseline entry and what it must contain, the interval for repeat entries, the items to describe for swelling, discharge, edge apposition, warmth and the patient's response to gentle palpation, the space for a value that allows comparison, for example a measured extent rather than the word large, and the two or three findings that trigger immediate escalation in writing. Self-review rubric: a colleague who has never met the patient can picture the wound from your entry alone, and your page contains no treatment instructions and no dose figures.
depth.summary: Post-operative complications are detected by comparison, not by diagnosis, and the technician's core product is a timed, descriptive baseline and its repeats, precise enough for a veterinarian to act on immediately. Published rates for complications such as anastomotic dehiscence are cohort properties that vary by procedure and by clinic, so they cannot be used to reassure an individual owner, but the variation itself shows that recording and detection practices are part of what a clinic's rate actually measures. Set against that, some findings compel an immediate, trained response, above all any suggestion of dehiscence or evisceration, where the correct action is protection, warm calm handling and immediate escalation. The result is a role that is simultaneously modest and consequential: describe, compare, protect, escalate, record, and leave interpretation and treatment where the law and the guidelines put them.
